identity.title: On Differential Privacy for Adaptively Solving Search Problems via Sketching

problem.claim: The paper studies differentially private mechanisms for answering adaptive search-problem queries while returning the solution itself.

gap.claim: Prior results covered numerical estimation and returned optimization costs rather than solutions, while adaptive search responses can reveal more about internal randomness.

contributions.claim: It develops differential-privacy-based algorithms for nearest-neighbor search and regression under arbitrary turnstile updates.
It relates memory and running time to problem parameters including the number of c-approximate near neighbors and the matrix condition number.
It reports similar tradeoffs for the two search problems.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish their focus on adaptive search problems that return solution points or vectors, extending the stated scope beyond numerical estimation and optimization-cost outputs.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report algorithms for nearest-neighbor queries and regression with arbitrary turnstile updates whose memory and time depend on identified problem parameters.
The authors report similar tradeoffs across the two problem settings.

narrative_sequence.summary: Differential privacy is presented as a way to support multiple adaptive queries without sacrificing response correctness.
Existing results show that some numerical estimation problems can tolerate T queries using Õ(√T) data-structure copies, returning optimization costs rather than solutions.
The paper turns to search problems, where responses may disclose more about internal randomness.
The study targets nearest-neighbor queries and regression with arbitrary turnstile updates.
It identifies governing parameters, designs privacy-based algorithms returning solutions, and reports similar tradeoffs between the tasks.

source_observation.claim: The abstract motivates the method by first isolating a limitation of prior problem and output types, then explicitly targets the missing search outputs.

lessons.interpretation: A contribution is easier to assess when the task, prior boundary, and extension are aligned.
lessons.application: Frame a new method by naming the exact prior output or problem class it does not cover, then state the corresponding output and setting your method handles.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when the work is primarily exploratory or when prior limitations cannot be stated precisely from available evidence.

unknowns: The abstract gives no quantitative tradeoff bounds, privacy parameters, query ranges, or comparison baselines for the proposed algorithms.
It does not specify the exact differential privacy techniques, approximation guarantees, or conditions under which correctness is maintained.

editorial_revisions.before: Existing results are described as requiring roughly the square root of the query count in data-structure copies, but only for numerical estimation and cost-only optimization outputs.
editorial_revisions.after: Existing results show that some numerical estimation problems can tolerate T queries using Õ(√T) data-structure copies, returning optimization costs rather than solutions.
editorial_revisions.note: Source-reviewed correction; initial generated response remains in local run logs.
